[[ja:社寺参詣曼荼羅]] [[sn:Temple and Shrine Pilgrimage Mandala]] {{translated page|ja|社寺参詣曼荼羅|version=99849361|comment=Imported full ja history}}

[[File:Kumano Nachi Mandala.jpg|thumb|400px|Nachi Pilgrimage Mandala (in the collection of {{ill|Kumano Nachi Taisha|ja|熊野那智大社|qq=draft|qq=draft}})]]
'''Shaji Sankei Mandara''' (社寺参詣曼荼羅) (also known as '''Jisha Sankei Mandara''' (寺社参詣曼荼羅) or simply '''Sankei Mandara''' (参詣曼荼羅)) is an academic term referring to religious paintings that depict {{ill|sacred site|ja|霊場|qq=draft|qq=draft}}s (namely, {{ill|Shinto shrine|ja|神社|qq=draft|qq=draft}}s and {{ill|temple|ja|寺院|qq=draft|qq=draft}}s) created for the purpose of inviting pilgrims and guiding them. In these works, many extant examples are simple and inexpensive paintings produced on paper with colored pigments, and they bear marks suggesting they were carried for proselytizing (see {{ill|Form|ja|形態|qq=draft|qq=draft}}). Several categories of earlier religious paintings have been pointed out as historical origins (see {{ill|Origin|ja|起源|qq=draft|qq=draft}}). Their formation is rooted in the fact that, after the {{ill|Sengoku period|ja|戦国時代|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, temples and shrines that could no longer depend on the protection of political power came to rely on the proselytizing activities of an external entity originally outside their walls, namely {{ill|Honganji|ja|本願 (日本史)|lt=Honganji|lt_ja=本願|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, and pilgrimage mandalas were employed as one of the means for such proselytizing (see {{ill|Establishment|ja|成立|qq=draft|qq=draft}}).
<ref>{{ill|Shimosaka 2003|ja|下坂[2003]|lt=Shimosaka 2003|lt_ja=下坂[2003]|qq=draft|qq=draft}}: 449, {{ill|Ohtaka 2012|ja|大高[2012]|lt=Ohtaka 2012|lt_ja=大高[2012]|qq=draft|qq=draft}}: 9</ref><ref>{{ill|Research History|ja|研究史|lt=Later discussion|lt_ja=後述|qq=draft|qq=draft}}</ref>
According to the organization by {{ill|Kazuo Tokuda|ja|徳田和夫|qq=draft|qq=draft}} (Tokuda [1990]: 24–25), the characteristics of pilgrimage mandalas are summarized in the following eight points, with particular emphasis on points 2 to 5:
{{Quotation| (1) They are painted with mud pigments on a large hanging scroll format (most are on paper, with only three on silk).
(2) They are clearly influenced by earlier mandalas depicting the honji, suijaku, and honjaku images as well as palace mandalas.
(3) They serve as objects of worship (worship paintings, Buddhist images, divine images).
(4) They provide an aerial view of the entire precincts (halls, towers, cloisters) of temples and shrines and their surroundings (maps).
(5) They arrange pilgrimage routes and depict the figures of pilgrims traversing them (guide maps, recreational maps).
(6) They often portray temple and shrine events, festivals, and the rituals of Buddhist and Shinto ceremonies as well as the prosperity of the gateway towns (landscape or genre paintings).
(7) They frequently incorporate narratives—origin stories and miracle accounts—passed down within temples and shrines (narrative, story, or didactic paintings).
(8) They are produced with the expectation of accompanying explanatory commentary (explanatory mandalas). | – Kazuo Tokuda, ''Egatarito Monogatari'' <ref>{{ill|Tokuda 1990|ja|徳田[1990]|lt=Tokuda 1990|lt_ja=徳田[1990]|qq=draft|qq=draft}}: 24–25</ref> }}
Although not every extant example exhibits all these features, taken together they provide a clear image of what pilgrimage mandalas are intended to represent<ref>{{ill|Ohtaka 2012|ja|大高[2012]|lt=Ohtaka 2012|lt_ja=大高[2012]|qq=draft|qq=draft}}: 37</ref>.
Approximately 150 examples of pilgrimage mandalas transmitted to the present are predominantly produced on paper<ref>{{ill|Ohtaka 2012|ja|大高[2012]|lt=Ohtaka 2012|lt_ja=大高[2012]|qq=draft|qq=draft}}: 36</ref>, painted using mud pigments such as vermilion, ultramarine, ochre, and gofun. They produce vivid, primary color effects, though their depiction techniques are simple<ref>{{ill|Fukuhara 1987|ja|福原[1987]|lt=Fukuhara 1987|lt_ja=福原[1987]|qq=draft|qq=draft}}: 214</ref>. Although there are silk examples, only 25 are known; among these, the {{ill|Tateyama Mandala|ja|立山曼荼羅|qq=draft|qq=draft}} accounts for 14, the majority of which are dated from the 19th century onward<ref>{{ill|Ohtaka 2012|ja|大高[2012]|lt=Ohtaka 2012|lt_ja=大高[2012]|qq=draft|qq=draft}}: 39–40</ref>.
The silk examples dating back to the period of the Tateyama Mandala are large scrolls unsuitable for portability, and were likely not removed from temple or shrine precincts<ref>{{ill|Ohtaka 2012|ja|大高[2012]|lt=Ohtaka 2012|lt_ja=大高[2012]|qq=draft|qq=draft}}: 40</ref>. However, the hanging scroll format was not necessarily the original form. Many paper examples transmitted in the hanging scroll format bear crease lines that suggest they were folded for transport<ref name="Ohtaka_2012_37"/>, and in some examples of {{ill|Nachi Sankei Mandala|ja|那智参詣曼荼羅|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, designs intended for suspension are also present<ref name="Ohtaka_2012_41">{{ill|Ohtaka 2012|ja|大高[2012]|lt=Ohtaka 2012|lt_ja=大高[2012]|qq=draft|qq=draft}}: 41</ref>, indicating that they were used as tools for proselytizing through explanatory narration which extolled the efficacies and benefits of the sacred site.
==Form and Origin== ===Form=== Many of the features characteristic of pilgrimage mandalas have been identified as described above. Although not every transmitted example possesses all of these characteristics, they collectively enable one to grasp the overall image of pilgrimage mandalas.
===Origin=== Historically, four categories of religious paintings have been considered as the antecedents of pilgrimage mandalas<ref>{{ill|Ohtaka 2012|ja|大高[2012]|lt=Ohtaka 2012|lt_ja=大高[2012]|qq=draft|qq=draft}}: 25, {{harvnb|Iwahana|1988}}</ref>. Specifically, the following four types are cited (for items 1–3, see {{ill|Fukuhara 1987|ja|福原[1987]|lt=Fukuhara 1987|lt_ja=福原[1987]|qq=draft|qq=draft}}: 214; for 4, see Shimosaka [2003]: 423–437): # Suijaku Mandala (palace mandala) # Temple and Shrine Origin Diagrams # Early Modern Genre Paintings # Temple and Shrine Diagrams
Among the Suijaku Mandalas, there are those depicting the descent of the original Buddha (honji mandalas) and those portraying the manifestation of deities (suijaku mandalas). In particular, those set against the backdrop of specific temples or sacred mountains are known as “palace mandalas” or “temple and shrine mandalas”, with examples known from {{ill|Kasuga Taisha|ja|春日大社|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, {{ill|Kumano Three Mountains|ja|熊野三山|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, and {{ill|Sannō Shrine (Hiyoshi Shrine)|ja|日吉大社|1=Hiyoshi Taisha|qq=draft|qq=draft|qq=draft}}. According to historical documents, their establishment dates back to the early medieval period, and they were produced during the {{ill|Kamakura period|ja|鎌倉時代|qq=draft|qq=draft}} and {{ill|Muromachi period|ja|室町時代|qq=draft|qq=draft}}<ref>{{ill|Ohtaka 2012|ja|大高[2012]|lt=Ohtaka 2012|lt_ja=大高[2012]|qq=draft|qq=draft}}: 33</ref>.
Temple and Shrine Origin Diagrams are picture scrolls that express the origin stories of temple and shrine establishments over time, employing a technique similar to that of emakimono by dividing the picture into segments to depict temporal progression<ref name="Iwahana_1988">{{harvnb|Iwahana|1988}}</ref>. They exist in both scroll and hanging scroll formats; initially, the scroll format was used, but later the hanging scroll format was adopted for the convenience of presenting to a larger audience. The inscriptions that accompanied the scroll versions were omitted in the hanging scroll versions, thus necessitating an intermediary to provide explanatory commentary. Among the extant examples, as with the Suijaku Mandalas, there are also silk examples that were not produced as inexpensive consumables<ref name="Ohtaka_2012_36">{{ill|Ohtaka 2012|ja|大高[2012]|lt=Ohtaka 2012|lt_ja=大高[2012]|qq=draft|qq=draft}}: 36</ref>.
In comparison, although Suijaku Mandalas similarly feature depictions of specific temples or sacred mountains and serve as objects of worship by portraying the descent of the original Buddha or the manifestation of deities, pilgrimage mandalas—which include depictions of honji and suijaku—do not predominantly represent these themes<ref name="Ohtaka_2012_34-35">{{ill|Ohtaka 2012|ja|大高[2012]|lt=Ohtaka 2012|lt_ja=大高[2012]|qq=draft|qq=draft}}: 34–35</ref>. Compared with Temple and Shrine Origin Diagrams, pilgrimage mandalas share the hanging scroll format and subject matter but are specifically designed for explanation to a broad audience. Moreover, while Temple and Shrine Origin Diagrams, like Suijaku Mandalas, are often produced on silk and are generally not inexpensive, the paper-based pilgrimage mandalas produced with mud pigments represent a stark contrast<ref name="Ohtaka_2012_36"/>. In pilgrimage mandalas, the iconography related to origin narratives is typically arranged along the periphery of the picture without a clear depiction of temporal progression, instead emphasizing a spatial representation of the sacred site<ref name="Iwahana_1988"/>. The depiction of pilgrims, particularly their recurring images, is a defining characteristic of pilgrimage mandalas, as these images encourage viewers to identify with the figures and emotionally engage with the sacred space.
===Establishment=== The establishment of pilgrimage mandalas is deeply linked to the role of Honganji. From ancient through medieval times, temples and shrines primarily depended on the patronage of institutions such as the imperial court or the shogunate; however, by the mid-15th century they could scarcely rely on such support<ref>{{ill|Shimosaka 2003|ja|下坂[2003]|lt=Shimosaka 2003|lt_ja=下坂[2003]|qq=draft|qq=draft}}: 431, {{ill|Ota 2008|ja|太田[2008]|lt=Ota 2008|lt_ja=太田[2008]|qq=draft|qq=draft}}: 160–161</ref> and instead came to depend on the proselytizing activities of {{ill|Honganji|ja|本願 (日本史)|lt=Honganji|lt_ja=本願|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, an entity originally external to the temples and shrines. This shift toward obtaining funding through external support can be traced back as early as the late 12th century and has been termed medieval proselytism<ref>{{ill|Nakanodou 2012|ja|中ノ堂[2012]|lt=Nakanodou 2012|lt_ja=中ノ堂[2012]|qq=draft|qq=draft}}: Chapter 1; {{ill|Shimosaka 2003|ja|下坂[2003]|lt=Shimosaka 2003|lt_ja=下坂[2003]|qq=draft|qq=draft}}: 189–190</ref>. Although medieval proselytism covered all aspects of temple reconstruction—from fundraising to rebuilding—it was essentially a temporary, emergency measure<ref>{{ill|Nakanodou 2012|ja|中ノ堂[2012]|lt=Nakanodou 2012|lt_ja=中ノ堂[2012]|qq=draft|qq=draft}}: 18–19, 120</ref>. For example, during the late-12th-century reconstruction of {{ill|Tōdai-ji|ja|東大寺|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, official positions were merely nominal while the actual work was carried out by the {{ill|Tōdai-ji Proselytism Office|ja|東大寺勧進職|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, making medieval proselytism the de facto contractor.
In contrast, Honganji was established on the premise of integrating proselytism into the temple and shrine system as a permanent activity. Not only did it engage in construction and repair, but it also aimed to participate in temple rituals and origin narratives in order to secure a permanent position within the institution<ref>{{ill|Shimosaka 2003|ja|下坂[2003]|lt=Shimosaka 2003|lt_ja=下坂[2003]|qq=draft|qq=draft}}: 217</ref>.
Pilgrimage mandalas were produced in large numbers primarily from the latter half of the 16th century to the 17th century. Their widespread creation is thought to be related to the activities of Honganji<ref>{{ill|Shimosaka 2003|ja|下坂[2003]|lt=Shimosaka 2003|lt_ja=下坂[2003]|qq=draft|qq=draft}}: 431, {{ill|Ohtaka 2012|ja|大高[2012]|lt=Ohtaka 2012|lt_ja=大高[2012]|qq=draft|qq=draft}}: 12</ref> as well as the network of sacred sites belonging to the {{ill|Nishikoku Sanjūsyo|ja|西国三十三所|1=Saigoku Kannon Pilgrimage|qq=draft|qq=draft|qq=draft}}. For these reasons, examples produced from the 18th to the 19th century (see below in the section on Early Modern Period) have often been excluded from the category of pilgrimage mandalas; however, contemporary research now includes works up to the 19th century as study subjects<ref>{{ill|Ohtaka 2012|ja|大高[2012]|lt=Ohtaka 2012|lt_ja=大高[2012]|qq=draft|qq=draft}}: 48–51</ref>.
In the pilgrimage narratives of the Muromachi period, there are many references to Kumano Gongen’s role, and the active promotion of the Sanjūsyo pilgrimage by Nachi Mountain of Kumano can be clearly seen<ref>{{ill|Fujisawa 1986|ja|藤沢[1986]|lt=Fujisawa 1986|lt_ja=藤沢[1986]|qq=draft|qq=draft}}: 4</ref>. Furthermore, as discussed later in the section on {{ill|Lineage Classification and Workshops|ja|系統分類と工房|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, several workshops are presumed to have been involved in the production of pilgrimage mandalas.
Pilgrimage mandalas were intended to serve in proselytizing, soliciting donations, or guiding pilgrims, and through these functions, they were used as instruments by Honganji to secure funds for temple repairs, construction, and daily offerings<ref>{{ill|Ohtaka 2012|ja|大高[2012]|lt=Ohtaka 2012|lt_ja=大高[2012]|qq=draft|qq=draft}}: 44–50</ref>. Although in many temples and shrines only a limited number were produced and used<ref>{{ill|Ohtaka 2012|ja|大高[2012]|lt=Ohtaka 2012|lt_ja=大高[2012]|qq=draft|qq=draft}}: 49</ref>, in the case of {{ill|Nachi Sankei Mandala|ja|那智参詣曼荼羅|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, numerous copies were transmitted<ref>These multiple copies, most of which are paper-based with nearly identical compositions, have been shown to belong to different lineages produced by several distinct workshops, as evidenced by variations in depiction techniques.</ref>. Similarly, there is another group of works—the {{ill|Tateyama Mandala|ja|立山曼荼羅|qq=draft|qq=draft}}—of which 48 examples are known, rivaling the Nachi Sankei Mandala in number.
==Spatial Composition of Temple and Shrine Pilgrimage Mandalas== {{external media | topic = Temple and Shrine Pilgrimage Mandalas | image1 = [http://www.kiyomizudera.or.jp/about/history.html Kiyomizudera Pilgrimage Mandala (partial)] | image2 = [http://www.kumadoco.net/kodo/img/report/event/14/ise_letter.gif Ise Pilgrimage Mandala] | image3 = [http://www.art-index.net/art_exhibitions/2009/09/62.html Ise Pilgrimage Mandala] | image4 = [http://www.pref.ishikawa.lg.jp/kyoiku/bunkazai/kaiga/k-22.html Colored-on-paper depiction of Kanazawa Castle town (Saikawaguchi-cho diagram) and a silk-colored depiction of Hakusan Mandala] | image5 = [http://www.pref.toyama.jp/branches/3044/exh_1102.htm Tateyama Mandala] }}
Pilgrimage mandalas were often created with the purpose of temple reconstruction<ref>{{ill|Ohtaka 2012|ja|大高[2012]|lt=Ohtaka 2012|lt_ja=大高[2012]|qq=draft|qq=draft}}: 39</ref> and, because immutability is one of the conditions for a site to be recognized as sacred<ref>{{ill|Shimosaka 2003|ja|下坂[2003]|lt=Shimosaka 2003|lt_ja=下坂[2003]|qq=draft|qq=draft}}: 452–453</ref>, they feature a distinctive spatial composition.
As a large-scale guide map<ref>{{harvnb|Iwahana|1996|p=127}}</ref>, pilgrimage mandalas depict in detail the sacred site, the pilgrimage routes leading to it, and the surrounding features (buildings, bridges, stone structures, etc.) as well as human figures<ref>{{ill|Shimosaka 2003|ja|下坂[2003]|lt=Shimosaka 2003|lt_ja=下坂[2003]|qq=draft|qq=draft}}: 460–461</ref>. In terms of composition, most examples are rendered in an aerial view that encapsulates the entire faith world of the temple or shrine in a single image. The use of ochre or gofun to fill the background suppresses the perception of depth, rendering the overall image uniformly flat; to compensate, some works depict pilgrimage routes or rivers in a zigzag pattern, employ clouds or mists to de-form distance, or insert horizontal steps along mountain paths to differentiate levels<ref>{{ill|Fukuhara 1987|ja|福原[1987]|lt=Fukuhara 1987|lt_ja=福原[1987]|qq=draft|qq=draft}}: 214</ref>. Whether this space possesses perspective has been a matter of debate<ref>{{ill|Kuroda 1986|ja|黒田[1986]|lt=Kuroda 1986|lt_ja=黒田[1986]|qq=draft|qq=draft}}: 108–110; {{ill|Nishiyama 1988|ja|西山[1988]|lt=Nishiyama 1988|lt_ja=西山[1988]|qq=draft|qq=draft}}: 111</ref>.
Another key compositional feature is the depiction of mountains in the upper portion of the image and the sea (or a river) in the lower portion<ref>{{ill|Fukuhara 1987|ja|福原[1987]|lt=Fukuhara 1987|lt_ja=福原[1987]|qq=draft|qq=draft}}: 214</ref><ref>{{ill|Nishiyama 1990|ja|西山[1990]|lt=Nishiyama 1990|lt_ja=西山[1990]|qq=draft|qq=draft}}: 60</ref>. In the sky, the sun and moon are depicted; in some cases (e.g. at Zenpōji or Tagasha) Venus or a crescent moon also appears. These paired celestial images symbolize day and night or the passage of time, signifying either the eternal nature<ref>{{ill|Fukuhara 1987|ja|福原[1987]|lt=Fukuhara 1987|lt_ja=福原[1987]|qq=draft|qq=draft}}: 215</ref> or the self-contained nature<ref>{{ill|Nishiyama 1990|ja|西山[1990]|lt=Nishiyama 1990|lt_ja=西山[1990]|qq=draft|qq=draft}}: 61</ref> of the sacred site – in other words, that it represents a complete microcosm<ref>{{ill|Nishiyama 1990|ja|西山[1990]|lt=Nishiyama 1990|lt_ja=西山[1990]|qq=draft|qq=draft}}: 70</ref>.
===Iconography of Sacred Sites and Pilgrimage Routes=== [[File:Nariaiji Sankei Mandala.jpg|thumb|250px|right|Jōsōji Sankei Mandala (with a depiction of Amanohashidate in the lower part)]] One of the conditions for a site to be considered sacred is its immutability, and pilgrimage routes leading to the sacred site often remain unchanged even today<ref>{{ill|Shimosaka 2003|ja|下坂[2003]|lt=Shimosaka 2003|lt_ja=下坂[2003]|qq=draft|qq=draft}}: 460</ref>. The immutability of a sacred site is not only a conceptual ideal; if a temple or shrine is damaged by human calamities (such as warfare) or by natural disasters (like lightning or heavy rains), restorative efforts are made to return it to its ideal state. Thus, the depictions in pilgrimage mandalas are rendered with considerable accuracy<ref>{{ill|Shimosaka 2003|ja|下坂[2003]|lt=Shimosaka 2003|lt_ja=下坂[2003]|qq=draft|qq=draft}}: 452, 460</ref>. However, since the depiction adheres to the concept of immutability, the sacred site as drawn may not reflect its actual appearance at the time of creation but rather an idealized form from the past or future<ref>{{ill|Ohtaka 2012|ja|大高[2012]|lt=Ohtaka 2012|lt_ja=大高[2012]|qq=draft|qq=draft}}: 39, 48</ref>.
For example, in the depiction of {{ill|Aogishido-ji|ja|青岸渡寺|1=Seiganto-ji|qq=draft|qq=draft|qq=draft}} in the Nachi Sankei Mandala, even after the temple was burned down in Oda Nobunaga’s campaign and subsequently reconstructed with pillar installations in June of Tenshō 15 (1735) at its current location, the mandala continued to depict Aogishido-ji as it was prior to June Tenshō 15<ref>{{ill|Ohtaka 2012|ja|大高[2012]|lt=Ohtaka 2012|lt_ja=大高[2012]|qq=draft|qq=draft}}: 101</ref>. In the Kiyomizudera Pilgrimage Mandala, a similar idealized depiction is made of {{ill|Gojo Bridge|ja|五条大橋|qq=draft|qq=draft}}. While contemporaneous copies of the Rakuchū Rakugai-zu depict Gojo Bridge with large abutments, every version of the Kiyomizudera Pilgrimage Mandala portrays it with red railings and golden {{ill|giboshi|ja|擬宝珠|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, expressing an idealized form<ref>{{ill|Shimosaka 2003|ja|下坂[2003]|lt=Shimosaka 2003|lt_ja=下坂[2003]|qq=draft|qq=draft}}: 150</ref>. Despite being an external feature, Gojo Bridge is not only idealized far beyond its actual appearance but is also allocated a prominent space in the depiction. This is likely due to its status as both the boundary of Rakuchū Rakugai and the departure point for the Kiyomizudera pilgrimage, as well as the special significance it held for Seijyūin—the Honganji of Kiyomizudera—charged with its maintenance and management<ref>{{ill|Shimosaka 2003|ja|下坂[2003]|lt=Shimosaka 2003|lt_ja=下坂[2003]|qq=draft|qq=draft}}: 191</ref>. In this way, the depiction of sacred sites adheres to the principle of immutability<ref>{{ill|Shimosaka 2003|ja|下坂[2003]|lt=Shimosaka 2003|lt_ja=下坂[2003]|qq=draft|qq=draft}}: 465–467</ref>. However, only those features that originally existed in an unchanging state are depicted in this idealized manner; for example, the Chōkuradō shown in the Kiyomizudera Pilgrimage Mandala is a later addition by Honganji for the temple’s reconstruction and does not retain an immutable form compared to its present-day appearance<ref>{{ill|Shimosaka 2003|ja|下坂[2003]|lt=Shimosaka 2003|lt_ja=下坂[2003]|qq=draft|qq=draft}}: 465–467</ref>.
In contrast, pilgrimage routes and sacred sites constitute distinct spaces and are depicted differently. In the Nachi Sankei Mandala, the area between Nachihama (the {{ill|Hama no Miya|ja|熊野三所大神社|qq=draft|qq=draft}}) and {{ill|Daimonzaka|ja|大門坂|qq=draft|qq=draft}} is significantly compressed compared to actual maps<ref>{{harvnb|Iwahana|1996|p=135}}</ref>. In order to accommodate the entire sacred site and to portray temple buildings with their southern facades, distortions occur in the depiction of distances and orientations; techniques such as using clouds and mists to segment the space are employed to de-form distance, evoking the viewer’s imagination of what lies beyond<ref>{{ill|Fukuhara 1987|ja|福原[1987]|lt=Fukuhara 1987|lt_ja=福原[1987]|qq=draft|qq=draft}}: 214</ref><ref>According to Nishiyama [1988], a version of the Kiyomizudera Pilgrimage Mandala estimated to date from the mid-16th century contains later additions of auspicious clouds deliberately used to distance the sacred site from the background mountain.</ref>. In the {{ill|Jōsōji Sankei Mandala|ja|成相寺参詣曼荼羅|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, which includes a depiction of {{ill|Amanohashidate|ja|天橋立|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, Amanohashidate is portrayed as bent so that the inner sea appears narrow. Additionally, in the {{ill|Shifukuji Pilgrimage Mandala|ja|施福寺参詣曼荼羅|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, the {{ill|Senju Kannon|ja|千手観音|qq=draft|qq=draft}} emerging from Osaka Bay is shown in the lower left of the image, with the roughly 20‐kilometer distance to the coast being compressed, and in the Kiyomizudera Pilgrimage Mandala the direction from which the {{ill|Kamogawa|ja|鴨川|qq=draft|qq=draft}} flows is bent 90° as if coming from the east<ref>{{harvnb|Iwahana|1996|p=135}}</ref>, resulting in similar distortions as seen in the depiction of temple buildings. Even when focusing on features within the sacred site, they are generally rendered without significant compression or distortion, serving instead as a faithful guide to the religious roles each element plays<ref>{{ill|Shimosaka 2003|ja|下坂[2003]|lt=Shimosaka 2003|lt_ja=下坂[2003]|qq=draft|qq=draft}}: 469</ref>. Thus, the basic principle is to render the sacred areas in detailed, large-scale precision while compressing the pilgrimage routes<ref>{{harvnb|Iwahana|1988|p=127}}</ref>.
===The Living World=== Within the picture, a diverse array of figures—including monks, predecessors, residents, and pilgrims—are depicted. In medieval picture scrolls, not only were social markers such as clothing used to denote status, but the spatial arrangement of figures also visibly conveyed the class structure<ref>{{ill|Kuroda 1982|ja|黒田[1982]|lt=Kuroda 1982|lt_ja=黒田[1982]|qq=draft|qq=draft}}: 66–67, 72–73</ref>, and similar expressions are found in pilgrimage mandalas. Frequently encountered figures include {{ill|Kōya Shō|ja|高野聖|qq=draft|qq=draft}} and {{ill|Biwa Hōshi|ja|琵琶法師|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, with the former usually positioned outside the sacred area demarcated by torii or gates, and the latter typically located along the periphery of the main hall. Such portrayals indicate that differences in status governed one’s proximity to the sacred<ref>{{ill|Iwahana 1988|ja|岩鼻[1988]|lt=Iwahana 1988|lt_ja=岩鼻[1988]|qq=draft|qq=draft}}: 136</ref>; in other words, it is not merely social hierarchy but also the structure of relationships with the sacred that is depicted<ref>{{ill|Iwahana 1988|ja|岩鼻[1988]|lt=Iwahana 1988|lt_ja=岩鼻[1988]|qq=draft|qq=draft}}</ref>.
In the {{ill|Nachi Sankei Mandala|ja|那智参詣曼荼羅|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, within the walled enclosure of Nachi Shrine – where only guardian dogs and crows appear – distinct spaces are delineated: the area between the wall and the main hall (where a noble figure resembling an imperial personage is shown), the main hall itself where temple priests and pilgrims congregate, the surrounding area where figures such as Biwa Hōshi and lay pilgrims gather, and even the area outside the gate where figures like {{ill|Kōya Shō|ja|高野聖|qq=draft|qq=draft}} are depicted<ref>{{ill|Iwahana 1996|ja|岩鼻[1996]|lt=Iwahana 1996|lt_ja=岩鼻[1996]|qq=draft|qq=draft}}: 136</ref>. In the Kiyomizudera Pilgrimage Mandala, between the first and second wooden gates along the pilgrimage route, there are depictions of outcasts and lepers<ref>{{ill|Shimosaka 2003|ja|下坂[2003]|lt=Shimosaka 2003|lt_ja=下坂[2003]|qq=draft|qq=draft}}: 151</ref>, and the overall composition is stratified according to social Rank<ref>{{ill|Iwahana 1996|ja|岩鼻[1996]|lt=Iwahana 1996|lt_ja=岩鼻[1996]|qq=draft|qq=draft}}: 136</ref>.
It is also customary for the same figure to be repeatedly depicted in different parts of the composition—a technique sometimes called the “same-time, same-image method”—thereby juxtaposing the figures progressing through the sacred space with the viewers who are addressed by the explanatory narration, inviting them to project themselves into the scene<ref>{{ill|Iwahana 1996|ja|岩鼻[1996]|lt=Iwahana 1996|lt_ja=岩鼻[1996]|qq=draft|qq=draft}}</ref><ref>See Kuroda [1986: 109] and {{ill|Nishiyama 1988a|ja|西山[1988a]|lt=Nishiyama 1988a|lt_ja=西山[1988a]|qq=draft|qq=draft}}: 120, 123–124; Ohtaka [2012: 38]</ref>. Moreover, in the Nachi Sankei Mandala the pair of figures dressed in white, initially depicted without explicit identification, eventually come to be shown explicitly as a married couple as time progresses. This change reflects shifts in the chronicling of popular life in the late medieval period<ref>Kuroda [1986: 123], Nishiyama [1988a: 128]</ref>, with later works increasingly featuring couples<ref>Nishiyama [1988a: 58–60]</ref>. In this way, the depiction of figures in pilgrimage mandalas expresses the “living world” of the time.
===Figures in Temple and Shrine Pilgrimage Mandalas=== In these works, sacred and secular figures are portrayed in several distinct scenes. Among the secular figures depicted along the pilgrimage route are the pilgrims themselves as well as local residents whose daily lives revolve around the route. These figures, also confirmed by other historical documents and artworks, are shown in their proper contexts<ref>{{ill|Shimosaka 2003|ja|下坂[2003]|lt=Shimosaka 2003|lt_ja=下坂[2003]|qq=draft|qq=draft}}: 462–464</ref>. Rather than being mere faithful copies, they represent idealized types—meticulously rendered images of the features and figures that pilgrims are expected to encounter<ref>{{ill|Shimosaka 2003|ja|下坂[2003]|lt=Shimosaka 2003|lt_ja=下坂[2003]|qq=draft|qq=draft}}: 464</ref>—and when depicted in a continuous sequence, they indicate the course of the pilgrimage<ref>{{ill|Nishiyama 1988a|ja|西山[1988a]|lt=Nishiyama 1988a|lt_ja=西山[1988a]|qq=draft|qq=draft}}: 123</ref>.
Conversely, figures portrayed in specific parts of the sacred space, along with their actions and gestures, indicate the unique significance of those areas. For example, a figure shown prostrating before a temple building clarifies the sacredness of the object of veneration<ref>{{ill|Nishiyama 1988a|ja|西山[1988a]|lt=Nishiyama 1988a|lt_ja=西山[1988a]|qq=draft|qq=draft}}: 123</ref>. These figures serve as guides to the religious significance of the sacred site, and when depicted together with the local features, they skillfully convey the efficacy and religious message of the place<ref>{{ill|Shimosaka 2003|ja|下坂[2003]|lt=Shimosaka 2003|lt_ja=下坂[2003]|qq=draft|qq=draft}}: 469</ref>. Thus, the array of secular figures enlivens the composition, allowing viewers of the explanatory narration to project themselves into the scene and, by mentally traversing the sacred space, reassemble the segmented image into the original sacred site<ref>Nishiyama [1988a: 120, 123–124]</ref>.
It is noteworthy that the iconography of secular figures is not unique to pilgrimage mandalas; common images such as those of {{ill|Biwa Hōshi|ja|琵琶法師|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, {{ill|Kōya Shō|ja|高野聖|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, and elderly women accompanying children appear ubiquitously in narrative artworks<ref>{{ill|Nishiyama 1987|ja|西山[1987]|lt=Nishiyama 1987|lt_ja=西山[1987]|qq=draft|qq=draft}}: 6–7</ref>, and frequently recurring figures (for example, Biwa Hōshi, Kōya Shō, and the aforementioned figures) are not exclusive to pilgrimage mandalas. For instance, the iconography of Biwa Hōshi can be traced from late Kamakura period craftsmen’s collaborative song paintings (e.g. “Tōhokuin Shokunin Utagai-e” or “Shichijūichi-ban Shokunin Utagai-e” circa 1500), through mid-12th-century works such as the “Nenchū Gyakuen Emaki”, “Ippen Shō-e” (1299), “Honen Shōnin Eden” (late Kamakura period), and “Fukutomi Zōshi” (early Muromachi period), showing a process of standardization<ref>Nishiyama [1987: 14–15]</ref>. Similar developmental processes can be observed in other figure types<ref>Nishiyama [1987: 16–19]</ref>. Moreover, one particular type of depiction of {{ill|Kōya Shō|ja|高野聖|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, in which one of a pair points forward while the other glances back, is found in 70–80% of pilgrimage mandala examples and is also seen in the Uesugi-bon version of {{ill|Rakuchū Rakugai-zu|ja|洛中洛外図|qq=draft|qq=draft}}<ref>Nishiyama [1987: 16–17]</ref>. These depictions of secular figures were arranged as collages of standardized images produced by early modern genre painting workshops<ref>Nishiyama [1987: 15–17]</ref>.
In contrast, there are also depictions of figures imbued with legendary or divine characteristics linked to sacred site origin narratives, which are unique to the sacred locale<ref>Nishiyama [1988a: 124], Shimosaka [2003: 470]</ref>; these figures are drawn at the periphery of the image<ref>{{ill|Shimosaka 2003|ja|下坂[2003]|lt=Shimosaka 2003|lt_ja=下坂[2003]|qq=draft|qq=draft}}: 470–471</ref>, such as the group related to the wandering ascetic Bunbaku in the Nachi Sankei Mandala, the child appearing riding a dragon at the foot of Fukase Bridge, the depiction of Enchin and a figure resembling Sakanotamura no Maro in the Kiyomizudera Pilgrimage Mandala, the Inugami Myōjin in the Tagasha Pilgrimage Mandala, the “Matsubiki no Matsu” and waterfall in the Kiminai-dera Pilgrimage Mandala, and even a monk seated opposite a dragon – to name but a few<ref>Shimosaka [2003: 471]</ref>. In pilgrimage mandalas, these figures function as guides: in the pilgrimage route they offer geographical and religious direction, while on the periphery they serve to introduce origin stories and legends<ref>Shimosaka [2003: 472]</ref>.
===Plants That Divide the Phases=== Pilgrimage mandalas frequently feature depictions of plants such as cedar, pine, cherry, maple, and evergreen broadleaf trees. These are not meant to represent actual vegetation but instead function as symbolic markers that segment the sacred from the secular space<ref>{{harvnb|Iwahana|1988|p=137}}</ref>. In medieval times, as seen in the Tengu Zōshi depicting Ippen’s dancing nembutsu, the most fitting expression of the Pure Land was a scene in which flowers fall. Such depictions of falling or scattering flowers evoked the Pure Land for the people of that era and signified that the work itself expressed the essence of the sacred site<ref>黒田 [1986: 114]. In the Kokugakuin, Nishifukujibon, and Takuhuke editions of the Nachi Sankei Mandala, cherry blossoms are depicted in the grove between the sun and moon at the top of the image, thereby emphasizing the Pure Land (Kuroda [1986: 114], {{ill|Nishiyama 1988a|ja|西山[1988a]|lt=Nishiyama 1988a|lt_ja=西山[1988a]|qq=draft|qq=draft}}: 111).</ref>
===Absence of Divine Images or the Principal Deity=== Despite being a painting of a sacred site, the mainstream examples of pilgrimage mandalas do not depict the original Buddha or the manifestation deities<ref>{{ill|Ohtaka 2012|ja|大高[2012]|lt=Ohtaka 2012|lt_ja=大高[2012]|qq=draft|qq=draft}}: 34–35</ref>. When they are depicted, a golden circular halo is used to represent the Buddha or deity, and in some cases a mandorla is drawn above to imply the presence of the original Buddha<ref>{{ill|Nishiyama 1988a|ja|西山[1988a]|lt=Nishiyama 1988a|lt_ja=西山[1988a]|qq=draft|qq=draft}}: 119</ref>. Examples that do depict the original Buddha or its equivalent include certain works of the {{ill|Tateyama Mandala|ja|立山曼荼羅|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, {{ill|Hakusan Mandala|ja|白山曼荼羅|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, and the {{ill|Fuji Pilgrimage Mandala|ja|富士参詣曼荼羅|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, as well as the {{ill|Kitano Shrine Mandala|ja|北野社|qq=draft|qq=draft}} and the Yoshino Mandala<ref>{{ill|Ohtaka 2012|ja|大高[2012]|lt=Ohtaka 2012|lt_ja=大高[2012]|qq=draft|qq=draft}}: 34–35</ref>. For instance, the main image of the original deity in the {{ill|Fuji Pilgrimage Mandala|ja|富士参詣曼荼羅|qq=draft|qq=draft}}—specifically, the {{ill|Fujisan Hongu Asama Taisha|ja|富士山本宮浅間大社|qq=draft|qq=draft}} version on silk (designated as an Important Cultural Property<ref>{{国指定文化財等データベース2|name=絹本著色富士曼荼羅図|register=201|item=2482|year=1977|jyear=昭和52|month=6|date=11|cat1=重要文化財|class=絵画|accessdate=2014-06-10}}</ref>)—bears a vase-shaped red seal by {{ill|Kanō Motonobu|ja|狩野元信|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, and is considered an early example of pilgrimage mandalas dating from the early 16th century<ref>{{ill|Ohtaka 2012|ja|大高[2012]|lt=Ohtaka 2012|lt_ja=大高[2012]|qq=draft|qq=draft}}: 237, 243</ref>. Similarly, an example influenced by the Kanō school is the {{ill|Atsuta Pilgrimage Mandala|ja|熱田社参詣曼荼羅|qq=draft|qq=draft}} (from the Tokugawa Art Museum), which, although it includes depictions of pilgrims, lacks narrative or miracle scenes and strongly retains the influence of preceding Suijaku or palace mandalas<ref>{{ill|Ohtaka 2012|ja|大高[2012]|lt=Ohtaka 2012|lt_ja=大高[2012]|qq=draft|qq=draft}}: 34–35, 243</ref>. These images, representing the principal deity or its equivalent<ref>{{ill|Nishiyama 1990|ja|西山[1990]|lt=Nishiyama 1990|lt_ja=西山[1990]|qq=draft|qq=draft}}: 61–61</ref>, are regarded as derivative in the context of pilgrimage mandalas and did not come to dominate<ref>{{ill|Ohtaka 2012|ja|大高[2012]|lt=Ohtaka 2012|lt_ja=大高[2012]|qq=draft|qq=draft}}: 35</ref>. This absence indicates that the layer which could visually control divine images was not inherent to the temple or shrine’s own power, but rather that pilgrimage mandalas were undertaken by the external force—Honganji—which was deliberately excluded from direct divine imagery<ref>{{ill|Nishiyama 1988a|ja|西山[1988a]|lt=Nishiyama 1988a|lt_ja=西山[1988a]|qq=draft|qq=draft}}: 119</ref>.
==Creators and Process== In the production of pilgrimage mandalas, the entity that conceived the creation of the painting—be it an individual, group, or organization—is referred to as the “creator.” Although there may be sponsors such as patrons or donors above the creator, it is the creator who commissions the work from a workshop (or painter) and receives the finished product; the user of the work does not necessarily coincide with the creator. This relationship is significant because medieval temple and shrine organizations were multi-layered, urban spaces that included not only formal members such as monks and pilgrims but also various external sacred figures and common people<ref>{{ill|Ohtaka 2012|ja|大高[2012]|lt=Ohtaka 2012|lt_ja=大高[2012]|qq=draft|qq=draft}}: 44</ref>. In proselytizing activities, those who used the work were often figures responsible for securing funds for repairs, construction, or offerings within the temple<ref>{{ill|Ohtaka 2012|ja|大高[2012]|lt=Ohtaka 2012|lt_ja=大高[2012]|qq=draft|qq=draft}}: 44–45</ref>.
Occasionally, a proselytizing saint—for example, one akin to Chūgen, who contributed to Tōdai-ji’s construction in the early Kamakura period—assumed full responsibility for everything from fundraising to construction and repair (a form of medieval proselytism)<ref>{{ill|Nakanodou 2012|ja|中ノ堂[2012]|lt=Nakanodou 2012|lt_ja=中ノ堂[2012]|qq=draft|qq=draft}}: 18–19, 120</ref>. Such medieval proselytism later became institutionalized within temples and shrines as the force known as {{ill|Honganji|ja|本願 (日本史)|lt=Honganji|lt_ja=本願|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, although it was never recognized as a formal part of the temple organization; as social stability improved in the early modern period, the original temple powers increasingly rejected Honganji, leading to its eventual decline<ref>{{ill|Shimosaka 2003|ja|下坂[2003]|lt=Shimosaka 2003|lt_ja=下坂[2003]|qq=draft|qq=draft}}: 216–217</ref>. Research on Honganji in relation to the Kumano Three Mountains and the Nachi Sankei Mandala has corroborated this view<ref>{{ill|Ohtaka 2012|ja|大高[2012]|lt=Ohtaka 2012|lt_ja=大高[2012]|qq=draft|qq=draft}}: 66</ref>, and the temple groups of Kumano Nachi Mountain, which served as the Honganji for the shrines, were guaranteed status and activities as the main temple bodies and dispatched throughout the country<ref>{{ill|Toshima 2005|ja|豊島[2005]|lt=Toshima 2005|lt_ja=豊島[2005]|qq=draft|qq=draft}}: 56, {{ill|Ota 2008|ja|太田[2008]|lt=Ota 2008|lt_ja=太田[2008]|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, among others such as {{ill|Toshima 1990|ja|豊島[1990]|lt=Toshima 1990|lt_ja=豊島[1990]|qq=draft|qq=draft}}</ref>. However, there are cases—such as at Kiyomizudera Seijyūin and Tagadaisha—where Honganji dominated the temple side, or where external proselytizing forces were not invited because funds could be procured internally; thus, the actual relationship between creator and user depends on the individual temple or shrine<ref>{{ill|Ohtaka 2012|ja|大高[2012]|lt=Ohtaka 2012|lt_ja=大高[2012]|qq=draft|qq=draft}}: 45–46</ref>.
===Nachi Mountain and the Temples of the Nishikoku Sanjūsyo=== [[File:Yoshiminedera Sankei Mandala.jpg|thumb|250px|right|Zenpōji Sankei Mandala]] The conventional understanding of pilgrimage mandalas is based on a model exemplified by 36 outstanding works—namely, the {{ill|Nachi Sankei Mandala|ja|那智参詣曼荼羅|qq=draft|qq=draft}}—and this view extends to the relationship between creator and user. The temple organization of Kumano Nachi Mountain consisted of temple families (the original formal members drawn from the local ruling class) and the Honganji, who, though not formal members, were expected to undertake proselytizing activities (known as the “Seven Hongan” or “Seven Grain Vendors”), which became established after the late 15th century<ref>{{ill|Ota 2008|ja|太田[2008]|lt=Ota 2008|lt_ja=太田[2008]|qq=draft|qq=draft}}: 180–181</ref>. In Nachi, the creator and the user coincide; similarly, in temples belonging to the Sanjūsyo, for example at Kiyomizudera where the Kiyomizudera Pilgrimage Mandala is housed, the creator and user are one and the same<ref>{{ill|Ohtaka 2012|ja|大高[2012]|lt=Ohtaka 2012|lt_ja=大高[2012]|qq=draft|qq=draft}}: 69</ref>. In both cases, the temple buildings established by Honganji within the sacred site are depicted in accordance with the respective origin stories, legends, or administrative functions, thereby asserting the identity of Honganji<ref>{{ill|Nei 2008|ja|根井[2008]|lt=Nei 2008|lt_ja=根井[2008]|qq=draft|qq=draft}}: 634; {{ill|Nishiyama 1988a|ja|西山[1988a]|lt=Nishiyama 1988a|lt_ja=西山[1988a]|qq=draft|qq=draft}}: 130–131; {{ill|Shimosaka 2003|ja|下坂[2003]|lt=Shimosaka 2003|lt_ja=下坂[2003]|qq=draft|qq=draft}}: 214–215</ref><ref>{{ill|Ohtaka 2012|ja|大高[2012]|lt=Ohtaka 2012|lt_ja=大高[2012]|qq=draft|qq=draft}}: 67, 69; {{ill|Shimosaka 2003|ja|下坂[2003]|lt=Shimosaka 2003|lt_ja=下坂[2003]|qq=draft|qq=draft}}: 214–215</ref>.
The {{ill|Kiminai-dera Sankei Mandala|ja|紀三井寺参詣曼荼羅|qq=draft|qq=draft}} was transmitted to {{ill|Kokuya-dera|ja|穀屋寺|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, the temple of the descendants of the grain vendors who once used it<ref>{{ill|Ohtaka 2012|ja|大高[2012]|lt=Ohtaka 2012|lt_ja=大高[2012]|qq=draft|qq=draft}}: 69</ref><ref>{{ill|Ohtaka 2012|ja|大高[2012]|lt=Ohtaka 2012|lt_ja=大高[2012]|qq=draft|qq=draft}}: 70</ref>. However, the main hall of Kiminai-dera—known as Gokokuin—originally belonged to Honganji dating back to the late 16th century, making it difficult to simply equate its relationship with that of temple families and Honganji; it is speculated that a bhikkhuni belonging to the grain vendor group possessed an image produced through the Honganji of the main temple<ref>{{ill|Ohtaka 2012|ja|大高[2012]|lt=Ohtaka 2012|lt_ja=大高[2012]|qq=draft|qq=draft}}: 216</ref>.
The {{ill|Funakawa-dera Sankei Mandala|ja|粉河寺参詣曼荼羅|qq=draft|qq=draft}} has two extant examples, one interpreted as a work produced after the late 16th century and the other after the early 18th century<ref>{{ill|Ohtaka 2012|ja|大高[2012]|lt=Ohtaka 2012|lt_ja=大高[2012]|qq=draft|qq=draft}}: 72</ref>. The depictions of temple buildings differ between these; in the former, a prominently large “Jukokubō” is depicted, whereas in the latter it is merely one of several structures. In Funakawa-dera, proselytizing was originally carried out by the Jukokubō from the late 15th century, but later, temple families (representing monastic figures) and lay pilgrims (representing itinerant figures) formed a “Sōbun” organization, replacing the earlier group—a change reflected in the differences in depiction<ref>{{ill|Ohtaka 2012|ja|大高[2012]|lt=Ohtaka 2012|lt_ja=大高[2012]|qq=draft|qq=draft}}: 72</ref><ref>{{ill|Ohtaka 2012|ja|大高[2012]|lt=Ohtaka 2012|lt_ja=大高[2012]|qq=draft|qq=draft}}: 165</ref>. Also, following restrictions imposed by the Edo Shogunate that curtailed unsanctioned proselytizing, there arose efforts to secure financial support from the Kii Domain<ref>{{ill|Ohtaka 2012|ja|大高[2012]|lt=Ohtaka 2012|lt_ja=大高[2012]|qq=draft|qq=draft}}: 168</ref>.
===Lineage Classification and Workshops=== Common stylistic and iconographic features are evident among the pilgrimage mandalas of the Sanjūsyo temples<ref>{{ill|Fujisawa 1990|ja|藤沢[1990]|lt=Fujisawa 1990|lt_ja=藤沢[1990]|qq=draft|qq=draft}}: 154</ref>. According to Takako Fujisawa’s survey of 22 examples from the Sanjūsyo temples and 22 examples from temples outside that group, aside from one notably small example of the Fuji Pilgrimage Mandala, most works exhibit similar dimensions or paper sizes, suggesting a standard format for a single sheet<ref>{{ill|Fujisawa 1990|ja|藤沢[1990]|lt=Fujisawa 1990|lt_ja=藤沢[1990]|qq=draft|qq=draft}}: 146</ref>. Moreover, when comparing the iconography within the images—the presence or absence of landscape elements, pilgrimage routes, and natural objects such as the sun, moon, or plants—common features are evident regardless of whether the temple belongs to the Sanjūsyo, indicating shared iconographic themes in pilgrimage mandalas<ref>{{ill|Fujisawa 1990|ja|藤沢[1990]|lt=Fujisawa 1990|lt_ja=藤沢[1990]|qq=draft|qq=draft}}: 149–150</ref>. Differences in the depiction of figures between early and later works suggest that a period of time was required for these images to become standardized<ref>{{ill|Fujisawa 1990|ja|藤沢[1990]|lt=Fujisawa 1990|lt_ja=藤沢[1990]|qq=draft|qq=draft}}: 151</ref>. In particular, the group comprising the Sanjūsyo temples and those including {{ill|Ise Shrine|ja|伊勢神宮|qq=draft|qq=draft}} and Tagasha can be distinguished by their unique treatment of figures<ref>{{ill|Fujisawa 1990|ja|藤沢[1990]|lt=Fujisawa 1990|lt_ja=藤沢[1990]|qq=draft|qq=draft}}: 151</ref>.
It is believed that multiple workshops were involved in the creation of pilgrimage mandalas, and researchers have attempted to classify them based on distinctive brushstrokes and techniques. Jō Nei, who attempted a classification of the Nachi Sankei Mandala, compared his results with those of {{ill|Nishiyama 1988b|ja|西山[1988b]|lt=Nishiyama 1988b|lt_ja=西山[1988b]|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, and identified one lineage—including the Tougō Shrine edition, the Okayama Takuhuke edition, the Kokugakuin scroll edition, and the Okayama Yoshida edition—and another lineage including the Nishifukujibon, the old Myōshin-ji edition, the Niigata Gotō edition, and the Sanda Dai Enji edition, which largely corresponded<ref>{{ill|Nei 2008|ja|根井[2008]|lt=Nei 2008|lt_ja=根井[2008]|qq=draft|qq=draft}}: 500–507</ref>. However, as Nei himself noted, the classifications of Nei and Nishiyama do not completely coincide, and there are differences in both the grouping and the criteria used.<ref></ref> Such classifications are not limited to Nachi; in pilgrimage mandalas from Ise and the Sanjūsyo temples as well, several workshops are presumed based on distinctive brushwork and stylistic features<ref>{{ill|Shimosaka 2003|ja|下坂[2003]|lt=Shimosaka 2003|lt_ja=下坂[2003]|qq=draft|qq=draft}}: 474–475; {{ill|Nishiyama 1988b|ja|西山[1988b]|lt=Nishiyama 1988b|lt_ja=西山[1988b]|qq=draft|qq=draft}}</ref>. The production period for these workshops is estimated to be the 16th century, and they established standardized techniques—such as filling the background with ochre<ref>{{ill|Shimosaka 2003|ja|下坂[2003]|lt=Shimosaka 2003|lt_ja=下坂[2003]|qq=draft|qq=draft}}: 476</ref>. Given that the works produced by these few workshops are widely distributed throughout the Nishikoku Sanjūsyo and that they possessed intimate knowledge of the local sacred sites, it is plausible to envisage a traveling collective of painters specializing in pilgrimage mandalas<ref>{{ill|Shimosaka 2003|ja|下坂[2003]|lt=Shimosaka 2003|lt_ja=下坂[2003]|qq=draft|qq=draft}}: 477</ref>. While opinions vary, it is generally considered that there were three to four principal workshops, whose works constitute a large proportion of the extant examples and played a leading role in standardizing the form<ref>{{ill|Shimosaka 2003|ja|下坂[2003]|lt=Shimosaka 2003|lt_ja=下坂[2003]|qq=draft|qq=draft}}: 476</ref>.
In these classifications, the lineage including the Nachi Sankei Mandala (from the Tougō Shrine edition) is believed to date back to at least the latter half of the 16th century. The Tougō Shrine edition is one of the few examples bearing a date inscription and is known for a repair inscription from Keichō 1 (1596)<ref>{{ill|Nei 2001|ja|根井[2001]|lt=Nei 2001|lt_ja=根井[2001]|qq=draft|qq=draft}}: 522</ref>. From an art historical perspective, the lineage of the Tougō Shrine edition has been identified as a series of types based on similar techniques shared with the {{ill|Hōkanji Pilgrimage Mandala|ja|法観寺参詣曼荼羅|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, {{ill|Shifukuji Pilgrimage Mandala|ja|施福寺参詣曼荼羅|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, {{ill|Jōsōji Pilgrimage Mandala|ja|成相寺参詣曼荼羅|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, Dōwakiji Pilgrimage Mandala, and {{ill|Zenpōji Pilgrimage Mandala|ja|善峯寺参詣曼荼羅|qq=draft|qq=draft}}<ref>{{cite book|author=Tsutada Tsutaka|chapter=社寺参詣曼荼羅図とその背景|editor2=Kyoto National Museum|year=1969|title=Koeizu|publisher=Kyoto National Museum}}</ref>.
===Pilgrimage Mandalas of Sacred Mountains=== Pilgrimage mandalas were also produced at many sacred sites and temples outside the Nishikoku Sanjūsyo. Among these, the {{ill|Tateyama Mandala|ja|立山曼荼羅|qq=draft|qq=draft}}—with 48 known examples—surpasses the Nachi Sankei Mandala’s 36 examples. At Tateyama, two temples (Iwashigami-ji and Ashigami-ji) formed pilgrimage communities; however, after prolonged debates over religious rights, a ruling by the Kaga Domain Public Office in Shōtoku 1 (1711) resulted in Iwashigami-ji monopolizing those rights, while Ashigami-ji became dependent solely on distributing pilgrimage plaques both within and outside the domain<ref>{{ill|Ohtaka 2012|ja|大高[2012]|lt=Ohtaka 2012|lt_ja=大高[2012]|qq=draft|qq=draft}}: 74</ref>. Under these circumstances, Ashigami-ji produced Tateyama Mandalas that were carried to various donor groups for explanatory narration; those with inscriptions indicating dates are all post-19th century<ref>{{ill|Ohtaka 2012|ja|大高[2012]|lt=Ohtaka 2012|lt_ja=大高[2012]|qq=draft|qq=draft}}: 75</ref>.
Compared with the Nachi Sankei Mandala, Tateyama Mandala shares the common purpose of soliciting pilgrimages and, notably, the establishment of a master–disciple (teacher–client) relationship between pilgrims and the guiding priests. However, Tateyama Mandala exhibits a greater diversity in composition<ref>{{ill|Ohtaka 2012|ja|大高[2012]|lt=Ohtaka 2012|lt_ja=大高[2012]|qq=draft|qq=draft}}: 52</ref>. Its various editions can be classified into those used by the Ashigami-ji group, those used by the Iwashigami-ji group, and those that do not belong to either group<ref>{{ill|Ohtaka 2012|ja|大高[2012]|lt=Ohtaka 2012|lt_ja=大高[2012]|qq=draft|qq=draft}}: 52</ref>. Although the Iwashigami-ji and other groups are thought to have originated as imitations of the Ashigami-ji works, differences in composition are evident, reflecting variations in proselytizing activities and religious ceremonies<ref>{{ill|Ohtaka 2012|ja|大高[2012]|lt=Ohtaka 2012|lt_ja=大高[2012]|qq=draft|qq=draft}}: 53</ref>. Moreover, Tateyama Mandala is notable for its depiction of the original Buddha or manifestation deities, as seen also in the pilgrimage mandalas of Hakusan, Fuji, Kitano Shrine, and Yoshino. Among these, Tateyama, Hakusan, and Fuji—revered as the “three mountains of Zen meditation”—were possibly intended for use within a limited circle<ref>{{ill|Ohtaka 2012|ja|大高[2012]|lt=Ohtaka 2012|lt_ja=大高[2012]|qq=draft|qq=draft}}: 35</ref>.
==Pilgrimage Mandalas in the Early Modern Period== Although the {{ill|Tateyama Mandala|ja|立山曼荼羅|qq=draft|qq=draft}} and {{ill|Hakusan Mandala|ja|白山曼荼羅|qq=draft|qq=draft}}—which together account for a majority of the 48 extant examples—have often been excluded from the category of pilgrimage mandalas (for example, the curator Toshio Fukuhara of the Osaka City Museum’s special exhibition regarded them as “Suijaku Mandalas with close kinship to pilgrimage mandalas” due to similarities in technique and composition, and they were not included in the exhibition catalog<ref>Fukuhara [1987]: 216</ref>), this was because Tateyama Mandala primarily originated in the latter half of the 18th century, coinciding with the decline of Honganji, the original creator of pilgrimage mandalas<ref>{{ill|Fukuhara 1987|ja|福原[1987]|lt=Fukuhara 1987|lt_ja=福原[1987]|qq=draft|qq=draft}}: 225</ref>. In other words, as temples and shrines became economically stable in the early modern period, they increasingly distanced themselves from Honganji, which led to its gradual exclusion<ref>{{ill|Shimosaka 2003|ja|下坂[2003]|lt=Shimosaka 2003|lt_ja=下坂[2003]|qq=draft|qq=draft}}</ref>.
This association between the decline of Honganji and the decline of pilgrimage mandalas has been modeled on the Nachi Sankei Mandala and its background in the Kumano Three Mountains Honganji<ref>{{ill|Ohtaka 2012|ja|大高[2012]|lt=Ohtaka 2012|lt_ja=大高[2012]|qq=draft|qq=draft}}</ref>. The explanatory narration originally delivered by the bhikkhuni associated with the Kumano Honganji is thought to have shifted its focus around the mid-17th century to the {{ill|Kumano Kankin Jikkai Mandala|ja|熊野観心十界曼荼羅|qq=draft|qq=draft}}<ref>{{ill|Nei 2008|ja|根井[2008]|lt=Nei 2008|lt_ja=根井[2008]|qq=draft|qq=draft}}: 641</ref>. Although this remains a hypothesis in the absence of concrete documentary evidence, this period is also considered a time when the institutionalization of pilgrimage mandalas advanced throughout the country, influenced by the Edo Shogunate’s religious controls, conflicts with temple families, or the expansion of the parish system<ref>{{ill|Ohtaka 2012|ja|大高[2012]|lt=Ohtaka 2012|lt_ja=大高[2012]|qq=draft|qq=draft}}: 52</ref><ref>{{ill|Nei 2008|ja|根井[2008]|lt=Nei 2008|lt_ja=根井[2008]|qq=draft|qq=draft}}: 648</ref>, and concurrently, pilgrimage mandalas transitioned from being merely proselytizing tools to objects of veneration in their own right, and at times were appreciated simply as works of art or decorative objects<ref>{{ill|Ohtaka 2012|ja|大高[2012]|lt=Ohtaka 2012|lt_ja=大高[2012]|qq=draft|qq=draft}}: 52</ref><ref>{{ill|Nei 2008|ja|根井[2008]|lt=Nei 2008|lt_ja=根井[2008]|qq=draft|qq=draft}}: 642</ref>. Yet, as evidenced by the survival of the Kumano Three Mountains Honganji until the modern period despite the separation of Shinto and Buddhism<ref>{{ill|Ota 2008|ja|太田[2008]|lt=Ota 2008|lt_ja=太田[2008]|qq=draft|qq=draft}}: 232</ref>, the course was not uniform and there were instances in which Honganji maintained its established position<ref>{{ill|Ohtaka 2012|ja|大高[2012]|lt=Ohtaka 2012|lt_ja=大高[2012]|qq=draft|qq=draft}}</ref>.
As described above, pilgrimage mandalas are paintings that depict sacred sites and serve to invite or guide viewers toward pilgrimage. While using these images to solicit pilgrimages or donations does not necessarily imply that the works were taken outside the temple or shrine, if the aim was to reach a broader audience, using them externally would have been even more effective<ref>{{ill|Ohtaka 2012|ja|大高[2012]|lt=Ohtaka 2012|lt_ja=大高[2012]|qq=draft|qq=draft}}: 50–51</ref>. Until the early modern period, the vast majority of commoners—who lacked the economic or social means to travel to distant sacred sites<ref>Kuroda [1986: 126], Fukuhara [1987: 225]</ref>—regarded reading talismans and listening to explanatory narration as equivalent in significance to actually visiting the sacred site<ref>{{ill|Shinjo 1982|ja|新城[1982]|lt=Shinjo 1982|lt_ja=新城[1982]|qq=draft|qq=draft}}: 102–109</ref>, and likely enjoyed pilgrimage mandalas accordingly<ref>Kuroda [1986: 126]</ref>.
Tateyama Mandala is similarly connected to this mode of enjoyment<ref>{{ill|Ohtaka 2012|ja|大高[2012]|lt=Ohtaka 2012|lt_ja=大高[2012]|qq=draft|qq=draft}}</ref>. From the early 18th century onward, Ashigami-ji of Tateyama, competing in the production of Tateyama Mandala, deepened its reliance on the distribution of pilgrimage plaques following a ruling in its dispute with Iwashigami-ji<ref>{{ill|Ohtaka 2012|ja|大高[2012]|lt=Ohtaka 2012|lt_ja=大高[2012]|qq=draft|qq=draft}}: 52</ref>. Its format eventually became that of a hanging scroll mounted on an axis for ease of storage and display, though it was not produced as an inexpensive consumable<ref>{{ill|Ohtaka 2012|ja|大高[2012]|lt=Ohtaka 2012|lt_ja=大高[2012]|qq=draft|qq=draft}}: 53</ref>. Tateyama Mandala continued to be produced to meet widespread demand and was expounded upon at various donor gatherings<ref>{{ill|Ohtaka 2012|ja|大高[2012]|lt=Ohtaka 2012|lt_ja=大高[2012]|qq=draft|qq=draft}}: 53</ref>. Whereas the Nachi Sankei Mandala—whose religious mission had concluded by the late 17th century—embodied “a painting carrying the rise and fall of Honganji”<ref>{{ill|Nei 2008|ja|根井[2008]|lt=Nei 2008|lt_ja=根井[2008]|qq=draft|qq=draft}}: 642</ref>, Tateyama Mandala, despite many similarities, had lost the itinerant, wandering character that is considered the essence of early pilgrimage mandalas<ref>{{ill|Fukuhara 1987|ja|福原[1987]|lt=Fukuhara 1987|lt_ja=福原[1987]|qq=draft|qq=draft}}: 225</ref>.
==Research History== Today, religious paintings categorized as temple and shrine pilgrimage mandalas are referred to by their holders as “ancient diagrams”, “picture scrolls”, or “cloister diagrams”<ref>{{ill|Ohtaka 2012|ja|大高[2012]|lt=Ohtaka 2012|lt_ja=大高[2012]|qq=draft|qq=draft}}: 38–39</ref>, and in early research they were collectively understood as ancient diagrams or Suijaku art<ref>{{ill|Ohtaka 2012|ja|大高[2012]|lt=Ohtaka 2012|lt_ja=大高[2012]|qq=draft|qq=draft}}: 9</ref>. A turning point in establishing them as an independent genre was the 1968 special exhibition “Ancient Diagrams” at the {{ill|Kyoto National Museum|ja|京都国立博物館|qq=draft|qq=draft}}. In that exhibition, the term “temple and shrine pilgrimage mandalas” was proposed to capture the nature and forms of the group of diagrams subsequently categorized as such. Particularly, the following year’s catalog<ref>{{ill|KNM 1969|ja|京都国立博物館[1969]|qq=draft|qq=draft}}</ref> featuring Tsuneo Takeda’s “Temple and Shrine Pilgrimage Mandala Diagrams and Their Background” was hailed as a seminal work in the research history, and was followed by Tetsu Naniwada’s ''Ancient Diagrams''<ref>{{ill|Naniwada 1972|ja|難波田[1972]|qq=draft|qq=draft}}</ref>, which introduced previously unfeatured works and broadened the scope of study<ref>{{ill|Ohtaka 2012|ja|大高[2012]|lt=Ohtaka 2012|lt_ja=大高[2012]|qq=draft|qq=draft}}: 10</ref>.
